title: The NewReno Modification to TCP's Fast Recovery Algorithm
summary: This RFC specifies the NewReno modification to TCP Fast Recovery, building on RFC 5681. It deals with partial acknowledgments, which cover new data but not all outstanding data, so several lost packets can be repaired in one recovery.

plainLanguage.summary: When a packet is lost, TCP resends it and cuts down how much it will send until the loss stops. With several packets lost at once, the classical rules can cut the window several times over or wait for a timeout. This RFC gives the sender one extra rule so that several losses in one window are repaired in a single recovery.

questions: how does newreno handle partial acks
what is the recover variable in newreno
subtitle: How a TCP sender without SACK repairs several lost packets in one window without timing out or shrinking its window again and again.

tldr.problem: In the classical Reno TCP, when several packets are lost from one window of data, the sender often ends up timing out, or performing several fast retransmits and several window reductions. Each of those costs throughput.
tldr.mechanism: NewReno adds one sender variable, recover, and a rule for what to do when an acknowledgment arrives that covers some but not all of the outstanding data: retransmit the next missing segment, shrink the congestion window by the amount newly acknowledged, and stay in fast recovery instead of starting over.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6582 is a Standards Track document from April 2012 that obsoletes RFC 3782. It applies to connections that cannot use the SACK option, and the RFC notes that the SACK option remains the better choice where it is available.

facts.label: Full ACK window rule
facts.value: min(ssthresh, max(FlightSize, SMSS) + SMSS) or ssthresh

facts.label: Fast recovery ends when
facts.value: An ACK acknowledges all data up to recover

today: RFC 6582 is a Standards Track document published in April 2012. It obsoletes RFC 3782, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. The RFC itself notes that the SACK option remains the better choice where it is available, since NewReno is for connections that cannot use it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 5681 documents four intertwined TCP congestion control algorithms: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery. It explicitly allows modifications of these algorithms, including ones that use the TCP Selective Acknowledgment option of RFC 2883, and ones that respond to partial acknowledgments, which are acknowledgments that cover new data but not all the data outstanding when loss was detected, in the absence of SACK. This document describes a specific algorithm for responding to partial acknowledgments, called NewReno, first proposed by Janey Hoe. It obsoletes RFC 3782.

In the typical implementation of the fast recovery algorithm of RFC 5681, first implemented in the 1990 BSD Reno release, the sender only retransmits a packet after a retransmit timeout or after three duplicate acknowledgments have arrived and triggered fast retransmit. A single timeout might cause several data packets to be retransmitted, but each invocation of fast retransmit leads to the retransmission of only a single data packet.

Two problems arise with Reno when multiple packet losses occur in a single window. Reno will often take a timeout, and even when a timeout is avoided, multiple fast retransmits and window reductions can occur. When multiple packets are lost and the SACK option is available, the sender has the information to make intelligent decisions about which packets to retransmit and which not to.

This document applies to TCP connections unable to use SACK, either because the option is not supported locally or because the peer did not indicate a willingness to use it. In the absence of SACK, little information is available to the sender during fast recovery: from the three duplicate acknowledgments it infers a packet loss and retransmits the indicated packet. In the case of multiple packets dropped from a single window, the first new information arrives when the sender receives an acknowledgment for the retransmitted packet. With a single drop and no reordering, that acknowledgment covers everything transmitted before fast retransmit was entered; with multiple drops it covers only some of it. That acknowledgment is called a partial acknowledgment.

The response described here is to infer that the next in-sequence packet has been lost and to retransmit it. The RFC does not claim that this is the optimal modification for connections that cannot use SACK, but based on experience with the network simulator ns-2 and with numerous implementations, the authors believe it improves the performance of fast retransmit and fast recovery in a wide variety of scenarios. Earlier versions of this document, RFC 2582 and RFC 3782, provide simulation-based evidence of the possible gains.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP normally resends one lost segment at a time and cuts its sending rate each time. If several segments from the same batch of data are lost, that means several cuts or a long wait. The rule here lets the sender keep repairing the same window until all the missing data has been acknowledged.

sections.title: Terminology and the recover Variable
sections.content:
The document assumes the reader is familiar with the terms SENDER MAXIMUM SEGMENT SIZE (SMSS), CONGESTION WINDOW (cwnd) and FLIGHT SIZE (FlightSize) defined in RFC 5681. SMSS is the largest segment the sender may transmit, cwnd is the limit the sender places on how much data may be outstanding, and FlightSize is the amount of data presently outstanding.

The document defines one additional sender-side state variable, recover. When the sender is in fast recovery, this variable records the send sequence number that must be acknowledged before the fast recovery procedure is declared to be over. When the TCP protocol control block is initialized, recover is set to the initial send sequence number.
sections.plainLanguage: The variable recover marks the point in the byte stream that the sender must reach before it can say the loss episode is over. It is set when fast recovery starts and updated when the sender times out.

sections.title: The NewReno Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery
sections.content:
The basic idea is that the sender can infer, from the arrival of duplicate acknowledgments, whether multiple losses in the same window of data have most likely occurred, and so avoid taking a retransmit timeout or making multiple congestion window reductions. The NewReno modification applies to the fast recovery procedure that begins when three duplicate acknowledgments are received and ends when either a retransmission timeout occurs or an acknowledgment arrives that acknowledges all of the data up to and including the data that was outstanding when the procedure began.

The procedures of Section 3.2 of RFC 5681 are followed with these modifications. On initialization, recover is set to the initial send sequence number. When the third duplicate acknowledgment is received, the sender first checks whether the Cumulative Acknowledgment field covers more than recover. If it does, the value of recover is incremented to the highest sequence number transmitted so far, and the TCP enters fast retransmit. If it does not, the TCP does not enter fast retransmit and does not reset ssthresh.

When an acknowledgment arrives that acknowledges new data, there are two cases. For a full acknowledgment, one that acknowledges all of the data up to and including recover, the sender sets cwnd to either min(ssthresh, max(FlightSize, SMSS) + SMSS) or to ssthresh, where ssthresh is the value set when fast retransmit was entered and FlightSize is the amount of data presently outstanding. This is called deflating the window. If the second option is chosen, the implementation is encouraged to avoid a possible burst of data, in case the amount of data outstanding in the network is much less than the new congestion window allows; a simple mechanism is to limit the number of data packets that can be sent in response to a single acknowledgment. The sender then exits fast recovery.

For a partial acknowledgment, one that does not acknowledge all of the data up to and including recover, the sender retransmits the first unacknowledged segment, deflates the congestion window by the amount of new data acknowledged by the Cumulative Acknowledgment field, and, if the partial acknowledgment acknowledges at least one SMSS of new data, adds back SMSS bytes to the congestion window. This artificially inflates the window to reflect the additional segment that has left the network. The sender sends a new segment if the new value of cwnd permits it. This partial window deflation attempts to ensure that when fast recovery eventually ends, approximately the ssthresh amount of data will be outstanding in the network. The sender does not exit fast recovery, so if any duplicate acknowledgments subsequently arrive, step 4 of Section 3.2 of RFC 5681 is executed. For the first partial acknowledgment that arrives during fast recovery, the retransmit timer is also reset.

After a retransmit timeout, the sender records the highest sequence number transmitted in recover and exits the fast recovery procedure if applicable. Because the acknowledgment field contains the sequence number that the sender next expects to receive, the acknowledgment covers more than recover when ack_number - 1 > recover, that is, when at least one byte more of data is acknowledged beyond the highest byte that was outstanding when fast retransmit was last entered.
sections.plainLanguage: When a full acknowledgment finally arrives, the sender puts its sending limit back to where it was before the loss, and leaves the recovery state. When only part of the missing data has been acknowledged, the sender resends the next missing piece, reduces its limit by the amount that was just acknowledged, adds one segment back, and stays in the recovery state instead of starting again.

sections.title: Duplicate Acknowledgments after a Timeout
sections.content:
After each retransmit timeout, the highest sequence number transmitted so far is recorded in recover. If, after a timeout, the sender retransmits three consecutive packets that the receiver has already received, it will receive three duplicate acknowledgments that do not cover more than recover. In that case the duplicate acknowledgments are not an indication of a new instance of congestion; they simply show that the sender has unnecessarily retransmitted at least three packets.

However, when a retransmitted packet is itself dropped, the sender can also receive three duplicate acknowledgments that do not cover more than recover, and in that case it would have been better off initiating fast retransmit. For a sender that implements this document's algorithm, the sender does not infer a packet drop from duplicate acknowledgments in this scenario, and the retransmit timer remains the backup mechanism for inferring packet loss.

Several heuristics, based on timestamps or on the amount of advancement of the Cumulative Acknowledgment field, allow the sender to distinguish in some cases between the two situations, and the TCP sender may use such a heuristic to decide to invoke a fast retransmit even when the three duplicate acknowledgments do not cover more than recover.

With the ACK heuristic, the sender stores the previous cumulative acknowledgment as prev_highest_ack and the latest as highest_ack, and performs an extra check when the Cumulative Acknowledgment field does not cover more than recover. If the congestion window is greater than SMSS bytes and the difference between highest_ack and prev_highest_ack is at most 4*SMSS bytes, the duplicate acknowledgments indicate a lost segment and the sender enters fast retransmit; otherwise they likely result from unnecessary retransmissions and it does not. The congestion window check protects against fast retransmit immediately after a retransmit timeout. The heuristic can fail if several acknowledgments are lost, because then the cumulative acknowledgment jumps by more than three segments.

With the timestamp heuristic, the sender stores the timestamp of the last acknowledged segment, and the check becomes: if the Cumulative Acknowledgment field did not cover more than recover, compare the echoed timestamp in the last non-duplicate acknowledgment with the stored timestamp. If they are equal, the duplicate acknowledgments indicate a lost segment and the sender enters fast retransmit; otherwise they likely result from unnecessary retransmissions. The heuristic works correctly when the receiver echoes timestamps as specified in RFC 1323 and by its revision attempts, but it can fail if the receiver arbitrarily echoes timestamps, or if a timeout was spurious and the returning acknowledgments are not from retransmitted segments, which can be prevented by detection algorithms such as the Eifel detection algorithm of RFC 3522.
sections.plainLanguage: After a timeout, three duplicate acknowledgments can mean two different things: that packets were genuinely lost, or that the sender resent packets the receiver already had. The RFC gives two ways to tell them apart, one by how far the acknowledgment number moved and one by comparing timestamps.

sections.title: Implementation Notes for Senders and Receivers
sections.content:
For the data receiver, RFC 5681 specifies that out-of-order data segments SHOULD be acknowledged immediately in order to accelerate loss recovery. Some receivers instead wait for their delayed acknowledgment timer to expire when they send a partial acknowledgment, which severely limits the potential benefit of NewReno by delaying the receipt of the partial acknowledgment at the sender. The recommendation is that the receiver send an immediate acknowledgment for an out-of-order segment, even when that out-of-order segment fills a hole in the buffer.

For the data sender, implementations are told to take measures to avoid a possible burst of data when leaving fast recovery, in case the amount of new data the sender may send under the new congestion window is large. Bursts can occur when the FlightSize is much less than the new congestion window on exit from fast recovery, which can arise during NewReno when acknowledgments are lost or treated as pure window updates. One simple mechanism is to limit the number of data packets that can be sent in response to a single acknowledgment, known as maxburst in ns-2. Other possibilities are rate-based pacing, or setting the slow start threshold to the resultant congestion window and then resetting the congestion window to FlightSize.

An implementation may want a separate flag to record whether it is presently in the fast recovery procedure; the duplicate acknowledgment counter is not reliable for that, because it can be reset on window updates and out-of-order acknowledgments. When updating the Cumulative Acknowledgment field outside fast recovery, the state variable recover may also need updating so that entry into fast recovery remains possible; this arises when an update results in a sequence wraparound that affects the ordering between the acknowledgment field and recover.

It is important for the sender to respond correctly to duplicate acknowledgments received when it is no longer in fast recovery, for example after a retransmit timeout. The Limited Transmit procedure of RFC 3042 describes possible responses to the first and second duplicate acknowledgments. When three or more duplicate acknowledgments are received, the Cumulative Acknowledgment field does not cover more than recover and a new fast recovery is not invoked, the sender should follow the guidance of Section 4; otherwise it could end up in a chain of spurious timeouts. The RFC mentions this only because several NewReno implementations had this bug, including the implementation in ns-2.

It has been observed that some TCP implementations enter a slow start or congestion avoidance window updating algorithm immediately after cwnd is set by the equation of Section 3.2, step 3, even without a new external event generating the change. After cwnd is set on the way out of fast recovery, cwnd should not be updated until a further event occurs, such as the arrival of an acknowledgment or a timeout.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things make the rule work. The receiver should acknowledge out-of-order data at once rather than waiting, so the sender learns quickly what is missing. The sender should avoid sending a burst of data when it leaves the recovery state, and it must not mistake duplicate acknowledgments left over from a timeout for fresh congestion.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: RFC 5681 discusses the general security considerations concerning TCP congestion control. This document describes a specific algorithm that conforms with the congestion control requirements of RFC 5681, so those considerations apply to it as well. There are no known additional security concerns for this specific algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule changes how the sender reacts to loss, not what is sent, so it adds no security risk of its own. The usual cautions about TCP congestion control apply.

sections.title: Conclusions and Changes since RFC 3782
sections.content:
This document specifies the NewReno fast retransmit and fast recovery algorithms for TCP. The modification can even be important for TCP implementations that support the SACK option, because the SACK option can only be used when both end nodes support it. NewReno performs better than Reno in a number of scenarios discussed in previous versions of the document.

The document says the important thing is to implement NewReno instead of Reno for a connection without SACK, and that it is less important exactly which variant of NewReno is implemented, because the differences between the variants are small compared with the difference between Reno and NewReno. Appendix A points back to the informative material in RFC 3782 on alternative behaviors for resetting the retransmit timer after a partial acknowledgment, for performing retransmission after a partial acknowledgment, for the motivation for the recover variable, for simulation test suites, for a comparison of Reno and NewReno, and for the changes relative to RFC 2582.

The change from RFC 3782 is in the value of cwnd on receipt of a full acknowledgment. In RFC 3782, cwnd after a full acknowledgment was set to min(ssthresh, FlightSize + SMSS) or to ssthresh. The first option carries a risk of performance degradation: if FlightSize is zero, the result is 1 SMSS, so TCP can transmit only one segment at that moment, which can cause a delay in acknowledgment transmission at the receiver because of a delayed acknowledgment algorithm. FlightSize on full acknowledgment reception can be zero in some situations, a typical example being a small sending window during fast recovery, where the retransmitted packet and new data packets can be transmitted within a short interval and the receiver may generate a full acknowledgment acknowledging all outstanding data; loss of acknowledgment packets or a receive buffer shortage during fast recovery can also increase the likelihood.

The fix in this document sets cwnd to at least 2*SMSS if the implementation uses the first option in the full acknowledgment case, so the sender transmits at least two segments on full acknowledgment reception. An erratum reported for RFC 3782, an editorial clarification to its Section 8, has been addressed in Section 6 of this document. The specification text of Section 3.2 was rewritten to track Section 3.2 of RFC 5681 more closely, and Sections 4, 5 and 9 to 11 of RFC 3782 were removed in favour of the new Appendix A.
sections.plainLanguage: The one technical difference from the previous version is that the sender now keeps enough of a window to send at least two segments when the loss episode ends, so that the receiver is not left waiting for an acknowledgment.

transitions.label: Three duplicate ACKs and ack_number - 1 > recover
Partial ACK: retransmit the first unacknowledged segment, deflate the window, stay in recovery
Full ACK: deflate the window and exit fast recovery

viz.caption: WHAT THE SENDER DOES WITH A FULL AND WITH A PARTIAL ACKNOWLEDGMENT

cells: Acknowledges all data up to and including recover. Set cwnd to min(ssthresh, max(FlightSize, SMSS) + SMSS) or to ssthresh, then leave fast recovery.

Does not acknowledge all data up to recover. Retransmit the first unacknowledged segment, deflate cwnd by the new data acknowledged, add back one SMSS if at least one SMSS was acknowledged, and stay in fast recovery.

data.title: Sender state changes
data.code:
ack_number - 1 > recover          ; does this ACK cover more than recover?

cwnd = min(ssthresh, max(FlightSize, SMSS) + SMSS)   ; or cwnd = ssthresh

cwnd = cwnd - (new data acknowledged) + SMSS   ; on a partial ACK

items.title: ack_number - 1 > recover
items.text: The test that decides whether the third duplicate ACK really covers new data.

items.title: recover
items.text: The sequence number that must be acknowledged before fast recovery is over. Raised when fast retransmit is entered and after a timeout.

items.title: ACK heuristic
items.text: After a timeout, treat duplicate ACKs as a loss if the cumulative ACK moved by at most 4*SMSS and the window is above SMSS.

items.title: Timestamp heuristic
items.text: After a timeout, treat duplicate ACKs as a loss if the echoed timestamp equals the stored timestamp of the last acknowledged segment.

items.title: Retransmit timer
items.text: Reset on the first partial ACK, and it stays the backup mechanism when the sender cannot tell a loss from an unnecessary retransmission.

items.title: maxburst
items.text: Limit how many segments may be sent for one acknowledgment, so leaving fast recovery does not produce a burst.
